vignette:
Mr. Adebayo presents as a man who wears his dignity like a well-tailored suit. At seventy-seven, his posture is still remarkably straight, a remnant of a lifetime spent commanding the respect of schoolchildren and their parents. For forty-two years, he has been a fixture at Northwood Elementary, the last twenty-five as its principal. He speaks of his school not as a workplace, but as a garden he has tended. He knows the name of every child, the squeak of every floorboard, the precise angle of the sun as it hits his office window in the late afternoon. His life, he explains, has always been built on order, predictability, and the quiet authority that comes from being a constant, reliable presence.

The foundation of that life crumbled on a Tuesday afternoon six months ago. It was a day like any other. He had gone to the bank to deposit a check, a simple errand he’d completed weekly for decades. On his walk back to his car, two young men approached him. He remembers the cold indifference in their eyes more than anything else. There was no argument, no preamble. One shoved him from behind, and as he stumbled, the other struck him across the face. He fell hard against the pavement, the rough concrete scraping his cheek and hands. They took his wallet and his watch—a retirement gift from the PTA a decade prior—and were gone in seconds. The physical injuries were minor: a split lip, deep bruising along his ribs, and scrapes that healed within a few weeks. The true damage was invisible.

In the weeks that followed, Mr. Adebayo insisted he was fine. He returned to work almost immediately, telling his concerned staff he was “sturdier than he looked.” But at home, his wife, Funke, saw the change. He stopped sleeping through the night, waking up gasping from dreams he refused to describe. He began locking and checking the doors obsessively, sometimes getting out of bed three or four times to rattle the deadbolt he knew was already secure.

The man who once walked his school’s hallways with an open, easy stride now hugs the walls. The sudden clang of a locker door or the sound of students running down the corridor makes his heart hammer against his ribs. He finds himself scanning the faces of parents and visitors, a cold knot of suspicion tightening in his stomach. He describes it as feeling like a foreigner in his own home. The school, once his sanctuary, now feels rife with unpredictable threats. He spends more time in his office with the door closed, a behavior so out of character that his secretary has asked him twice if he is feeling unwell.

Intrusive images of the assault punctuate his days. While signing a permission slip, he’ll suddenly see the impassive face of his attacker or feel the phantom sensation of the cold pavement against his cheek. He feels a profound and gnawing shame, a sense of humiliation that a man his age, a community leader, could be so easily overpowered. This shame has built a wall between him and Funke. He can’t stand her worried glances, interpreting them as pity. He feels a persistent numbness, a detachment from the things that once brought him joy. The laughter of the children in the schoolyard, a sound he once cherished, now feels distant and irritating.

He has started taking different, longer routes to and from work to avoid the street where it happened. He no longer goes on the evening walks he and his wife have shared for fifty years. Retirement is looming, a milestone he once anticipated with pleasure. Now, the thought of unstructured days, of more time alone with his thoughts, fills him with a quiet dread. He feels like an actor playing the part of Principal Adebayo, going through the motions of a life that no longer feels like his own.
